The prompt arrives like a gift wrapped in fog: a thousand words, no map, no destination. I feel the weight of the limit not as a cage but as a riverbank—something to push against so the current has shape. What comes first? The smell of old paper, yes, that always comes first, followed by the sound of a distant train that might be real or might be the memory of a train I never rode. I think of the word “threshold” because every sentence is one. I am already crossing.

A room appears. It has windows facing north, and the light there is always blue, not gray but a specific kind of blue that makes one think of underwater cities long abandoned by their architects. On the table sits a glass of water that is not water but liquid time, and a clock that ticks backward because it is tired. I do not know why I invented these objects, except that free writing is archaeology of the immediate—digging up what you buried five seconds ago. The clock ticks once. The water ripples. I write about them because they are here, and “here” is the only honest place.

Memory is an unreliable narrator. I remember a kitchen in Lisbon where someone was peeling apples with a knife that had a wooden handle shaped like a bird. Did this happen? It feels true in the way fiction feels true—through texture, not evidence. The apples were yellow, and the peel came off in long spirals that looked like handwriting in a language I almost recognize but not quite. I wanted to ask the person peeling them what they were writing, but they were already gone, replaced by the sound of a bicycle bell that rings in my left ear whenever I think of Portuguese tiles. I do not correct the error. I let it stand.

Time is not linear; it is a collage. I am writing this at a moment that might be morning or might be the middle of a Tuesday in 1997, or perhaps a Tuesday that never existed until this sentence called it into being. The distinction does not matter because the words are being born now, in this specific now that contains all other nows. I think of the number 1000 and its weight: ten centuries, a millennium, a thousand small deaths of attention. Each word is a step across a dark room. I do not need to see the floor to take the step. I need only the willingness to fall.

What else? A list, because lists are democratic and they ask for nothing in return:
- The sound of a page turning in a windstorm.
- A dog that only barks at mirrors.
- The color purple, which is actually a disagreement between red and blue.
- A sentence that begins with “If only” and ends in a different language entirely.
- The idea that every unfinished thought is a kind of inheritance left to strangers.

These are not metaphors, though they could be. They are just things that arrived, like birds on a windowsill, and I am allowing them to stay until I decide they are insects and quietly remove them.

I imagine a conversation between two people who have never met, speaking through the medium of this text. One says: “I am afraid of the silence after the last word.” The other replies: “Then write more slowly.” This is advice I try to follow, though speed is tempting because the word count presses gently at my back like a kind teacher who insists on homework but does not punish delay. I slow down. I describe the texture of the screen I am writing on—cool, slightly abrasive, a surface that holds heat like a promise made in good faith. The promise is that this will end, and that the ending will not be a failure.

There is a philosophy of the mundane that I have just invented in the space of a breath. It holds that brushing your teeth is a form of archery: the brush is the bow, the teeth are the target, and the paste is the arrow that never quite reaches, dissolving instead into foam and purpose. I like this because it makes the ordinary heroic without demanding a stage. I apply it to writing: each word is a toothbrush, and the page is the mouth of reality, and we are all just cleaning out the cavities of our understanding, trying to prevent decay in an organism that does not ask for our care.

Sensory details accumulate like snow against a windowpane. The smell of rain on asphalt—petrichor, that beautiful word—mixes with the taste of metal that comes before a storm in certain cities where the air is thick and brown. I am not in a storm now, but I can feel it gathering at the edges of my attention like a crowd at the end of a long hall. There is a dog in this narrative now, a black dog with one white paw, and it is sleeping on a rug that depicts the map of a country that does not exist. The dog dreams of swimming. I do not question the imaginary geography. I only note the paw, the rug, the dream, and move on, which is how we survive the unreal.

Language is a river that flows backward through us. Every word I use has been used before, often in grief, often in joy, always in some human mouth that is now silent or buried in earth. I am a temporary vessel for old sounds. This is not humility; it is physics. The words “come to me” because they are already here, circulating in the air like pollen, and I capture them in the net of this paragraph. Some escape through the mesh. Some stick to the threads. The ones that stick become part of the count, part of the thousand, part of the architecture of this particular moment that will soon be past.

I should talk about the ending, because everything ends, even this slowly unfolding thought. The thousand words will become a finite thing, a block of text with a bottom edge and a slight silence after it. I imagine someone reading this far, possibly at 2 AM, possibly on a phone in a waiting room with fluorescent lights that hum, possibly never at all but that is okay because the act of writing is its own audience and needs no witness to justify its existence. I want to leave them with the sound of the clock from earlier, ticking backward, or with the blue light of the north-facing window, or with the smell of apples and bird-shaped knives.

Actually, I will end with a return to the prompt: “Write whatever comes to you.” It came to me that freedom is not the absence of limits but the presence of a limit generous enough to hold your shape without crushing it. I have used them, and they have used me; we have worn each other down to the essential grain. The last word is “threshold,” because every ending is a threshold, and every threshold is an invitation to cross toward something else—something I will not name now, because naming it would make it a cage, and I have enough of those. I cross now. The door closes. The water ripples one final time. The clock stops.
